A trout is a type of fish. More specifically, it is a freshwater fish — meaning it lives in rivers, streams, and lakes (not the sea), though a few types can spend time in saltwater too.

Trout belong to the salmon family, which means they are close relatives of salmon. They share many qualities: a streamlined, torpedo-shaped body built for swimming in fast-moving water, and a similar life cycle in some cases.

Trout are medium-sized fish, typically anywhere from 20 cm to over 90 cm long, depending on the species and how well-fed they are. They have:

  • A sleek, smooth body tapering at both ends
  • Spots or speckles on their body — often black, red, or orange dots, sometimes with a halo around them
  • A small, fleshy extra fin on the back near the tail (called an adipose fin — a feature shared with salmon and a few other related fish)
  • Firm, slightly oily flesh that ranges from white to pink to deep orange-red in color depending on diet

They are generally considered beautiful fish, prized for their vivid patterns.

The most important thing to understand about trout is that they are demanding about their environment. They need:

  • Cold water — most species thrive between 10°C and 16°C. Warmer temperatures stress or kill them.
  • Clean, clear water — they cannot survive in polluted or murky water.
  • Well-oxygenated water — fast-flowing streams and rivers are ideal because moving water picks up oxygen from the air.

Because of this, trout are often used as an indicator species — if trout are living in a river, the water is clean and healthy. If they disappear, something is wrong with the ecosystem.

They are found naturally across North America, Europe, and parts of Asia, but have been introduced to rivers and lakes all over the world (including South America, New Zealand, South Africa, and India) for sport fishing.

Trout are carnivores (meat eaters). They are active hunters and eat:

  • Insects — both aquatic insects (such as mayflies, caddisflies, and stoneflies, often as larvae under water) and flying insects that fall onto the water's surface
  • Worms and small invertebrates
  • Small fish — larger trout will readily eat smaller fish, including younger trout
  • Crustaceans (such as freshwater shrimp) and sometimes frogs or small amphibians

Trout have sharp eyesight and are known to be cautious and intelligent for a fish, which is part of why catching them is considered a skill.

There are many species of trout. The most commonly known ones are:

Rainbow trout — Probably the most well-known in the world. It has a distinctive pink or reddish stripe running along its side, with black spots on a silver or greenish body. Originally native to the western coast of North America, it has been introduced globally. It is also the most widely farmed trout and the most common trout you'll find in a supermarket or restaurant.

Brown trout — Native to Europe and western Asia. It has a golden-brown to olive body covered in dark spots, often with reddish or orange spots surrounded by pale rings. It is known for being particularly wary and difficult to catch.

Brook trout — Native to eastern North America. It is often considered one of the most beautiful freshwater fish, with a stunning pattern of red dots surrounded by blue halos on its sides, and vivid orange-red fins edged with black and white. Despite being called a "trout," it is technically a char (a close relative within the salmon family).

Lake trout — A large species found in deep, cold lakes in North America. It can grow very big, sometimes exceeding 10 kg.

Cutthroat trout — Native to western North America, named for the distinctive red or orange slash marks on either side of the jaw, as if the throat has been cut.

Sea trout — Not a separate species but a form of the brown trout that migrates to the sea and returns to freshwater to breed, similar to how salmon behave.

Trout has been eaten by humans for thousands of years and remains a popular food today. It is widely regarded as:

  • Delicious and nutritious — it is rich in protein and omega-3 fatty acids (healthy fats)
  • Versatile in the kitchen — it can be baked, pan-fried, grilled, smoked, or poached
  • Milder than salmon — people who find salmon too rich or oily often prefer trout

Rainbow trout is the species most commonly farmed and sold in markets. Smoked trout is a particularly popular delicacy in Europe.

Trout are one of the most celebrated sport fish (fish that are fished for the thrill of catching, not just for food) in the world. Fly fishing — a technique where a lightweight artificial lure called a "fly" is cast onto the water to mimic an insect — was essentially developed around trout fishing. It is considered an art form and has a long, rich cultural tradition, especially in Britain and North America.

Trout fishing requires patience, skill, and an understanding of the fish's behaviour. Catching a large, wild trout in a cold mountain stream is considered one of the great experiences in angling (the hobby of fishing with a rod and line).

In many countries, trout rivers and streams are carefully managed, with rules about fishing seasons, minimum sizes, and limits on how many fish you can keep, in order to protect the population.

The plural of trout follows an interesting rule:

  • When you are talking about more than one fish of the same species, the plural is simply "trout" (no change). For example: "I caught five trout today." This is similar to how "fish" is used as its own plural.
  • When you are talking about multiple different species together, you can say "trouts." For example: "The river holds rainbow trouts, brown trouts, and brook trouts." However, this usage is less common in everyday speech.

In practice, "trout" (unchanged) is the form you will encounter most of the time.

In British English, "trout" is also used informally — and somewhat unkindly — to describe a bad-tempered, unpleasant, or foolish old woman. It is usually phrased as "old trout." For example: "Don't be such an old trout." This usage is old-fashioned and not particularly common today, but you may come across it in older British literature or television. It has nothing to do with the fish itself — the connection is unclear — and is simply an insult rooted in British slang.

A trout is a beautiful, spotted, cold-water fish closely related to salmon, valued both as a food and as a prized catch for sport fishermen. It needs exceptionally clean, cold, oxygen-rich freshwater to survive, and its presence in a river is a sign of a healthy ecosystem. There are many species — rainbow, brown, brook, lake, cutthroat being the most notable — each with its own distinctive look and home range. It is delicious to eat, rich in healthy fats, and central to the tradition of fly fishing. And, rarely, in older British speech, it is also a mildly rude word for a grumpy old woman.
